0.0.n: Introduces a contrast with what was said before.

0.1.n: Softens the opening and draws the listener in.

0.3.n: Pairs with から言うと to introduce the bottom line.

0.4.n: Marks the starting point: the conclusion comes first.

0.5.n: The plain form combines with と in the expression 結論から言うと.

0.6.n: With 言う, forms an introduction meaning to put it a certain way.

0.8.n: Strengthens 問題なく, emphasizing the complete absence of problems.

0.9.n: Combines with なく to describe trouble-free use.

0.10.n: なく is the linking form of ない; 問題なく describes how something can be used.

0.11.n: The ability form of 使う says the keyboard is usable.

0.12.n: Adds a reflective feeling to the thought quoted before 思いました.

0.13.n: A conversational form of という that introduces the content of the speaker’s thought.

0.14.n: In っていうふうに, frames the preceding statement as the speaker’s impression.

0.15.n: Makes ふう describe the manner of thinking.

0.16.n: Polite past form of 思う, reporting the impression the speaker reached.

1.0.n: Introduces the first aspect the speaker will discuss.

1.1.n: Adds a friendly, conversational pause after まず.

1.3.n: Refers to how the keyboard looks, including its printed markings.

1.4.n: だ changes to な before explanatory ん after a noun.

1.5.n: Short for の, framing the appearance as the topic being explained.

1.6.n: The plain linking word completes the explanatory expression なんだ.

1.7.n: Gently introduces the topic here rather than expressing a strong contrast.

1.9.n: 版 means version or edition, here referring to a keyboard made for Japanese.

1.10.n: Presents Japanese versions as an example rather than an exhaustive category.

1.11.n: Combines with と to introduce the case of Japanese versions.

1.12.n: After だ, sets up what applies when the keyboard is a Japanese version.

1.14.n: Refers to the keyboard area the speaker is indicating.

1.15.n: Marks the location where the characters are printed.

1.16.n: This is a mistaken split of ひらがな, the name of a Japanese script; it is not ひる.

1.17.n: This が belongs inside ひらがな and is not a separate particle.

1.18.n: This な completes ひらがな and is not a form of ない.

1.19.n: Marks ひらがな as what is written on the keyboard.

1.20.n: 書く in て-form plus ある describes writing that has been put there and remains visible.

1.21.n: The preceding phrase describes a keyboard with hiragana printed on it.

1.22.n: With なる, marks the resulting type or configuration.

1.23.n: Short for なっている, describing the keyboard’s current configuration rather than an ongoing change.

1.24.n: Stands for products with the keyboard configuration just described.

1.25.n: Indicates that versions of this kind exist among other possibilities.

1.26.n: Says that some products have this configuration.

1.27.n: Short for の, adding explanatory background before です.

1.28.n: Makes the explanation polite in んです.

1.29.n: A softer, more formal alternative to けど that leads into the speaker’s contrasting choice.

2.0.n: Explicitly identifies the speaker as the person making the choice.

2.1.n: Marks 私 as the topic, contrasting the speaker’s choice with the versions just mentioned.

2.2.n: Points back to the type of keyboard markings previously described.

2.3.n: Combines with そういう and に to refer to markings appearing in that manner.

2.4.n: Makes そういうふう describe how characters appear on the keyboard.

2.5.n: Refers to Chinese-language markings on the keyboard.

2.6.n: Gives Chinese as an example of additional language markings.

2.7.n: Marks 中国語とか as what is not included.

2.8.n: Casual shortening of 入っていない, describing the absence of those markings.

2.10.n: Refers to the alphabet used for English, rather than Japanese or Chinese characters.

2.11.n: Limits the keyboard’s markings to alphabet letters.

2.12.n: Links アルファベットだけ to もの, describing the kind of item chosen.

2.13.n: Stands for the keyboard or product selected.

2.14.n: Marks the item as what the speaker chose.

2.15.n: Polite past form of 選ぶ, reporting a completed selection.

3.0.n: Connects this explanation to the preceding description.

3.1.n: The plain form directly describes 所 as a point that differs.

3.2.n: Refers to a point of difference, not necessarily a geographical place.

3.3.n: Marks what is being mentioned in the expression と言えば.

3.4.n: The conditional form of 言う combines with と to mean speaking of.

3.6.n: Points to the specific keyboard area being discussed.

3.7.n: Politely identifies this spot as the relevant difference.

3.8.n: Softens the identification and invites the listener’s attention.

3.10.n: Refers to entering text in a selected language.

3.11.n: Links input to switching: the switching concerns the input language.

3.12.n: A noun from 切り替える, referring to changing between input languages.

3.13.n: Links switching to the button used for that function.

3.14.n: Refers to the keyboard control for changing input languages.

3.15.n: Connects the button with the area or part being discussed.

3.16.n: This combines ところ with subject-marking が; it is not the conjunction meaning however.

3.18.n: Names one language in the expected input-switching pair.

3.19.n: Joins Japanese and English as a pair.

3.20.n: Names the second language in the expected pair.

3.21.n: The linking form of だ begins ではなくって, which rejects the preceding language pair.

3.22.n: Forms part of ではなくって, contrasting the expected pair with the actual pair.

3.23.n: Conversational form of なくて, linking the rejected option to its replacement.

3.25.n: Names the language offered instead of Japanese on this button.

3.26.n: Joins Chinese and English as the actual pair.

3.27.n: The language shared by both the expected and actual pairs.

3.28.n: Marks the resulting setting with なる.

3.29.n: Short for なっている, describing the current language configuration.

3.30.n: Downplays the difference by saying it amounts to roughly this much.

3.31.n: The linking form of だ leaves the explanation open to continue in the next line.

0.lit: But, you know, speaking from the conclusion, I thought in this way: it can be used completely without problems.
0.tip: 使える is the ability form of 使う: the speaker found the keyboard usable, not merely that they used it.

1.lit: First, appearance-wise, with Japanese versions and such, there are also ones configured as keyboards with hiragana written here, but…
1.tip: 書いてある describes writing that someone put there and that remains visible.

2.lit: As for me, I chose one without Chinese and such included that way, with only alphabet letters.
2.tip: Both 入ってない and アルファベットだけの describe もの, the item the speaker chose.

3.lit: So, speaking of differing parts, here: the input-switching button is Chinese and English, not Japanese and English—that’s about it…
3.tip: ではなくって contrasts two options: not Japanese and English, but Chinese and English.
